sections.body: Several sources describe rendering strategies that make large or expensive visual computations tractable by spreading, merging, or reusing work. Amortized temporal sampling smooths a reprojected running average to reduce variance over time, while graph level-of-detail rendering merges node work into pixel bins and aggregates edges or endpoints in image space.
sections.heading: Section 1

sections.body: The common concept is controlled loss or approximation in service of interactive rendering. Temporal amortization trades noise reduction against lag or blur; graph aggregation trades individual detail for density fields, cluster-level connectivity, and scalable overview rendering.
sections.heading: Section 2

sections.body: This topic is synthesis-worthy because both sources use screen-space or frame-buffer-oriented computation to avoid work proportional to every original sample at full fidelity. The supporting evidence is strongest when framed around performance and approximation trade-offs, not identical algorithms.
